query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Tailored severe thermo‐mechanical processing that refines the eutectic lamellar colonies into an ultrafine duplex microstructure will simultaneously improve both room-temperature tensile strength and ductility in eutectic high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) having coarse dual-phase lamellar colonies with extensive internal boundaries that are prone to initiating microcracks during room-temperature deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a severe thermo‐mechanical process—such as cold rolling followed by controlled, partial annealing—to refine the lamellar spacing while preserving a dual-phase (hard and soft) structure.
generation.conditions: Processing and testing at room temperature, with parameters chosen to avoid full recrystallization so that the duplex (refined and retained coarse) microstructure is maintained and the two phases are kept in balance.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultrafine duplex microstructure characterized by significantly refined lamellar spacing and maintained/developed internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The refinement leads to increased strength through Hall-Petch grain boundary strengthening, while the enhanced and well-distributed internal boundaries act as effective microcrack arresters, thereby delaying catastrophic crack propagation and increasing tensile ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline processed by conventional casting methods, the treated alloy will display a significant increase in both yield/ultimate tensile strength and elongation at failure during room-temperature deformation.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high-entropy alloys produced by conventional processing that yield coarse lamellar colonies and exhibit limited ductility due to microcrack initiation and propagation.
generation.boundary: The processing must retain the dual-phase equilibrium (i.e., the coexistence of the hard and soft phases) and must avoid complete recrystallization which would eliminate the beneficial internal boundaries; the optimized processing parameters (e.g., degree of cold work, annealing temperature/time) are critical and must be within a window that preserves the lamellar integrity.
generation.uncertainty: Exact processing conditions (degree of cold rolling, annealing temperature, and duration) that optimally balance the refinement and phase stability are not yet determined, and the interplay between grain refinement and microcrack arrest mechanisms under different strain rates may vary.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same eutectic high-entropy alloy composition: one set processed by conventional casting and the other processed via the proposed severe thermo‐mechanical treatment (cold rolling followed by controlled partial annealing). Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and use microscopic techniques (e.g., SEM, TEM) to compare the microstructural features (lamellar spacing, grain size, and internal boundary characteristics) as well as the macroscopic mechanical properties.
measurements: Lamellar spacing and grain size (from SEM/TEM)
Fractography analysis to identify microcrack arrest features
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the conventionally processed baseline, or if microscopic analysis fails to reveal a refined duplex microstructure with evidence of microcrack arresting features, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Enhanced strength–ductility synergy in ultrafine-grained eutectic high-entropy alloys by inheriting microstructural lamellae

Abstract: Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism.
